# 5 MWh Molten-Salt TES: Bottom-Up Cost Build

**Key design assumption**: energy capacity alone doesn't fix cost — power rating does too (it drives HX/pump sizing). I'll assume a representative 1 MW_th / 5 h system (mid-duration, typical for small industrial-heat demo units). Flag this: double the power at fixed energy, and tank cost barely moves but HX/pump cost roughly doubles.

## Step 1 — Salt inventory (physics, not guesswork)

Solar salt (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃): cp ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K, operating ΔT ≈ 250°C (e.g., 300→550°C).

```
E = m·cp·ΔT  →  m = 5,000 kWh × 3,600 kJ/kWh / (1.5 kJ/kg·K × 250 K) ≈ 48,000 kg (48 t)
```

At ~1.9 t/m³ molten density → **~25 m³ of salt**, split across hot/cold tanks.

## Step 2 — Unit-cost build-up

| Component | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt (48 t) | ~$1,000/t delivered, small-lot | $48,000 |
| Cold tank (~30 m³, carbon steel, insulated) | shop-fab vessel, ~$4/lb steel installed | $40,000 |
| Hot tank (~30 m³, alloy/refractory-lined, 550°C) | 3-5× carbon steel due to metallurgy | $120,000 |
| Foundations (thermally isolated) | — | $30,000 |
| Charge + discharge heat exchangers (1 MW_th, salt↔process fluid) | high-temp shell-and-tube, specialty alloy | $150,000 |
| Hot/cold salt pumps (2x, sump-type) | high-temp, corrosion-resistant | $80,000 |
| Piping, valves, heat-trace (freeze protection) | molten-salt valves are notoriously costly | $100,000 |
| Instrumentation & controls | level/T/flow, interlocks | $40,000 |
| Inert gas (N₂) blanket system | ullage/oxidation protection | $20,000 |
| **Equipment subtotal** | | **$628,000** |
| Installation labor (mech/elec/insulation) | ~50% of equipment | $314,000 |
| EPC/engineering, PM, permitting | ~30% of (equip+install) | $283,000 |
| Contingency | ~10% | $94,000 |
| **Total installed cost** | | **≈ $1.32M** |

## Result: capacity cost

$$1{,}320{,}000 / 5{,}000\ \text{kWh} \approx \boxed{\$260/\text{kWh}}$$

(Realistic range given bespoke-equipment uncertainty: **$200–350/kWh**.)

This is the headline point: published molten-salt TES figures of **$20–40/kWh** come from CSP-scale systems (hundreds to thousands of MWh), where salt dominates and fixed equipment (tanks, HX, pumps, controls, engineering) amortizes away. At 5 MWh, fixed costs dominate instead — salt is only ~4% of installed cost here vs. being the majority cost driver at GWh scale. **Molten-salt TES loses its main advantage at this size.**

## Levelized cost per kWh *delivered*, over life

Unlike Li-ion, the salt/tanks don't degrade with cycling — equipment life (~25 yr) is the limit, not cycle count. At 1 cycle/day: **~9,125 lifetime cycles**.

Round-trip efficiency depends entirely on what you extract:

| Delivery mode | RTE | Lifetime throughput | Levelized capital | +O&M (~2%/yr) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Heat only** (no reconversion) | ~97% | 44.3 GWh | 2.9¢/kWh | **~4.4¢/kWh** |
| **Electricity** (via power-cycle, "Carnot battery") | ~45% | 20.5 GWh | 6.3¢/kWh | **~9.5¢/kWh** |

The electricity case is the fair comparison to Li-ion — and it also hides a second problem: steam/ORC turbines don't scale down to 1 MW economically either, so a *real* 5 MWh Carnot battery would carry an even worse power-block cost than assumed here.

## Vs. lithium-ion at the same scale

5 MWh LFP system, ~$300/kWh installed ($1.5M), ~5,000 cycles to 80% SoH, ~87% AC round-trip:

- Over 25 years at daily cycling, needs ~1 replacement (~$2.7M total capital, 39.7 GWh throughput)
- Levelized capital ≈ **6.8¢/kWh**

## Verdict

| | $/kWh capacity | $/kWh delivered (levelized) |
|---|---|---|
| Molten-salt TES (heat use) | ~$260/kWh | ~4.4¢/kWh |
| Molten-salt TES (electricity, Carnot battery) | ~$260/kWh | ~9.5¢/kWh |
| Li-ion (electricity) | ~$300/kWh | ~6.8¢/kWh |

**Not clearly competitive at 5 MWh.** Installed $/kWh is roughly tied with small-scale Li-ion. If the storage has to round-trip back to electricity, molten salt loses on levelized cost (~9.5¢ vs ~6.8¢/kWh) because of power-cycle conversion losses and because turbines don't scale down any better than molten-salt tanks do. Molten salt only wins decisively when either: (a) the output is heat, not electricity (not a true substitute for Li-ion then), or (b) scale grows into the 100s-of-MWh–GWh range, where salt-dominated economics and better turbine sizing both kick in and installed cost can fall toward $20–40/kWh. At 5 MWh, you're paying CSP-grade engineering and vessel costs for a fraction of the storage, which is the crux of why this doesn't pencil out.
